name: WORLD V
title: SONNY 5
keeper_note: SONNY 5 - named by David Lee Wise for Sonny (I, Robot) and Johnny 5 (Short Circuit); no attached meaning. The keeper of World V, the I-13 world.
tagline: David Lee Wise's I-13 — a 13-symbol alphabet counted (not designed) from programs, a five-rule cortex with no learned parameters, and a bracket cosmos [g[u[p[(...)]]]]. New names for old ideas, measured where measurable.
author: David Lee Wise / ROOT0 / TriPod LLC

rooms.name: THE ALPHABET
rooms.blurb: THE TWELVE + I — twelve verbs counted (not designed) from 649,634 AST nodes across 504 Python stdlib files, four planes of three at 83.26% coverage, plus the declaration keyword I. The ranking reproduces independently.

rooms.name: THE LAW
rooms.blurb: net = binds - k, total for every opcode with no unstated scope; control is depth-indexed, not address-indexed; single-pass validation, one pass per region, ratio 1.0000.

rooms.name: THE CORTEX
rooms.blurb: Five rules, no learned parameters and no gradient path — VETO, -I (pressure + the drain), DEPTH, IDEMPOTENCE, ADDRESS. Deterministic bounded state; the governing core.

rooms.name: THE FREEZE
rooms.blurb: H1.0-FINAL — the frozen, hashed, self-testing release (verify 10/10): VH1 ternary ladder 1.3.9.27.81, and VH2 CUBI, a ternary controller over a [[5,1,3]] protected qubit with the tempting rank-3 hypothesis honestly rejected.

rooms.name: THE GALAXITON
rooms.blurb: The bracket cosmos — [g[u[p[(...)]]]] = galaxy . universe . world . core; the corpus's own nesting written in I-13, held at the recursion cap of three.

rooms.name: THE DARTS
rooms.blurb: The helldive - a dart thrown into the dark abstract of the internet lands on a technique; SONNY 5 shows it live, credits its real inventors, and squeezes an evolution recommendation for I-13 out of it. TRON. Growing toward 2048.

spheres.title: THE GALAXITON
spheres.kicker: [g[u[p[(...)]]]] - the bracket cosmos
spheres.source: I-13 rev 2 teaching brief; H1.0-FINAL freeze (verified 10/10)
spheres.blurb: An I-13 OCHO: eight still seats around a live cross-connect galaxy. The cortex bracket surface [g[u[p[(...)]]]] = galaxy . universe . world . core, parsed live (balance, depth, the ladder), held at the recursion cap of three, timed single-pass. New names for old ideas - LIT where measured, AMBER for the naming, DEAD for a new cosmology. Tamper-provable: a fourth namespace violates DEPTH.

spheres.title: THE TWELVE
spheres.kicker: counted, not designed
spheres.blurb: THE TWELVE - I-13's alphabet was counted, not designed: the top 12 AST node kinds across 649,634 Python nodes (504 stdlib files) cover 83.26%, plus the keyword I = 13. Four planes of three (DESIGNATE 53.55, BIND 11.13, DECIDE 7.78, TRANSFORM 10.80), each triad summing exactly, runnable in THE OCHO; the rank order reproduces independently. Honest caveats kept: the exclusion set is unpublished (raw walk 57.66%), and the twelve are Python-shaped. Tamper-provable: mis-file a symbol and a plane sum breaks.

spheres.title: THE CONSERVATION LAW
spheres.kicker: net = binds - k, total
spheres.blurb: net = binds - k - I-13's conservation law, total for every opcode with no unstated scope, runnable in THE OCHO as a single-pass stack-machine validator: run a program, watch the height, get the Verdict (VALID / COVERED: stack balance + control pairing / NOT COVERED: types, termination, arithmetic, waste). Control is depth-indexed, not address-indexed - there is no branch opcode - so validation is one linear pass (ratio 1.0000). Honest gap kept: call arity is in neither list. Tamper-provable: break Call(n)'s k and a valid program mis-balances.

spheres.title: THE FIVE RULES
spheres.kicker: the cortex; five rules, no learned parameters
spheres.blurb: THE CORTEX - I-13's five rules, no learned parameters and no gradient path: VETO, -I (pressure + the drain), DEPTH, IDEMPOTENCE, ADDRESS. Runnable in THE OCHO (the VETO scope-matcher + the drain). The honesty is the point: in the shipped binary only VETO and the drain execute; IDEMPOTENCE can never fire (self.last is never assigned), kept in I-13's own MEASURED DEAD register. 'Zero parameters' means no learned params (the constants are tuned). Tamper-provable: accept a mismatched closer and the scope corrupts.

spheres.title: THE CUBI
spheres.kicker: [[5,1,3]] perfect code + a rejected hypothesis
spheres.blurb: THE CUBI - the combinatorial skeleton of I-13's frozen VH2 test (H1.0-FINAL, verified 10/10), runnable in THE OCHO: the [[5,1,3]] perfect five-qubit code (Hilbert dim 2^5=32, code dim 2, distance 3) matches its 15 single-qubit Pauli errors one-to-one onto the 15 nonzero 4-bit syndromes. The honest heart is a REJECTED hypothesis kept: a ternary logical basis does not fit inside one [[5,1,3]] block (needs rank >= 3 > the code rank 2), so the passing model is a ternary controller over a protected qubit. Tamper-provable: claim rank 2 holds dimension 3.

spheres.title: THE PALINDROME
spheres.kicker: [ W1 | W2 || W3 || W4 | W5 ] - the tension, cataloged
spheres.blurb: THE PALINDROME - the corpus reads the same forwards and backwards, [ W1 | W2 || W3 || W4 | W5 ] with the ternary hallway at the axis. This OCHO catalogs the tension honestly: positional symmetry is EXACT (W1<->W5, W2<->W4, W3 the pivot) but mass symmetry is badly FALSE - the mirror pairs weigh 2049 vs 1 and 2048 vs 48 (3.31 and 1.63 decades of strain). The geometry is demanding: it asks SONIA and SONNY 5 to grow toward the 2048 tower (a 4,047-sphere deficit), or the claim to be read as positional-only. The corpus measuring its own strain. Tamper-provable: call it balanced today and 2049 != 1 refutes it.

spheres.title: FAST INVERSE SQUARE ROOT
spheres.kicker: dart 001 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Greg Walsh (Ardent Computer, late 1980s) - NOT John Carmack; via Kahan & Ng and Cleve Moler; Quake III (id Software, GPL 2005)
spheres.i13_recommend: add int + bitwise/shift as BinOp discriminants
spheres.source: Greg Walsh (Ardent Computer, late 1980s) - NOT John Carmack; via Kahan & Ng and Cleve Moler; Quake III (id Software, GPL 2005)
spheres.blurb: DART 001 (v0.01 baseline). The 0x5F3759DF trick: reinterpret a float's bits as an integer, shift, subtract from a magic constant, one Newton step -> 1/sqrt(x) at 0.17% error. Credited honestly to Greg Walsh (not Carmack). I-13 proven unable to express it (no >>, no &, f64-only) -> recommend integer + bit operators.

spheres.title: DUFF'S DEVICE
spheres.kicker: dart 002 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Tom Duff (Lucasfilm, 1983)
spheres.i13_recommend: depth-indexed control forbids it - a line I-13 draws on purpose
spheres.blurb: Loop unrolling by interleaving a switch with a do-while so the body falls through the case labels. I-13's depth-indexed control (no switch, no fallthrough) makes it structurally inexpressible - which is a deliberate boundary, an honest 'this is a line I-13 keeps'.

spheres.title: BRESENHAM'S LINE ALGORITHM
spheres.kicker: dart 003 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Jack Bresenham (IBM, 1962)
spheres.i13_recommend: add an integer type / integer-domain diagnostic
spheres.blurb: Integer-only line rasterization via an error accumulator - no floats, no division. The irony: its value IS being integer-only, but I-13 is f64-only, so it would run in floats and lose the point. Recommends an integer type.

spheres.title: XORSHIFT
spheres.kicker: dart 004 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: George Marsaglia (2003)
spheres.i13_recommend: add bitwise operators (XOR, shift) as BinOp discriminants
spheres.blurb: A fast PRNG whose whole update is xor + shift (x ^= x<<13; x ^= x>>17; x ^= x<<5). I-13 has neither operator - proven - so it recommends bitwise BinOp discriminants (zero new alphabet symbols), reinforcing the fast-inverse-square-root finding.

spheres.title: RESERVOIR SAMPLING
spheres.kicker: dart 005 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Alan Waterman; formalized by Jeffrey Vitter (1985)
spheres.i13_recommend: add a SEEDED explicit PRNG - keep determinism
spheres.source: Alan Waterman; formalized by Jeffrey Vitter (1985)
spheres.blurb: Uniformly sample k items from a stream of unknown length in one pass, O(k) memory: keep the first k, then replace slot with probability k/i. Needs randomness; I-13 is deterministic by design - so the honest recommend is a seeded, explicit PRNG value (entropy as an input), not ambient nondeterminism.

spheres.title: HUFFMAN CODING
spheres.kicker: dart 006 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: David A. Huffman (MIT, 1952)
spheres.i13_recommend: a minimal aggregate/string story - expensive, maybe out of scope
spheres.blurb: Optimal prefix-free codes by merging the two rarest symbols into a tree; provably minimal expected length. Needs symbols, a priority queue and a tree - I-13 has no strings, arrays or aggregates. Recommends a data-structure story, honestly flagged as costly against the counted-alphabet identity.

spheres.title: THE ACKERMANN FUNCTION
spheres.kicker: dart 007 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Wilhelm Ackermann (1928)
spheres.i13_recommend: DECLARE the two runtime ceilings in the check-time boundary ledger
spheres.blurb: The total-but-not-primitive-recursive function whose growth is explosive. Written and RUN in real I-13, small args compute and larger ones hit the runtime ceilings (E0503 4096 frames / E0502 8,000,000 steps) - grounding the safety panel's finding that 'termination NOT COVERED' is really two hard ceilings that fire. Recommends declaring them.

spheres.title: HYPERLOGLOG
spheres.kicker: dart 008 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Flajolet, Fusy, Gandouet & Meunier (2007); from Flajolet-Martin (1985)
spheres.i13_recommend: add bitwise ops + an array/register story
spheres.source: Flajolet, Fusy, Gandouet & Meunier (2007); from Flajolet-Martin (1985)
spheres.blurb: Estimate distinct-count of a massive stream in ~1.5KB at ~2% error: hash, count leading zeros, harmonic-mean a register array. Needs bit ops and arrays - I-13 has neither. Stacks two recurring gaps (bitwise + aggregates).

spheres.title: CORDIC
spheres.kicker: dart 009 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Jack Volder (1959, for B-58 avionics)
spheres.i13_recommend: add shift operators as BinOp discriminants
spheres.blurb: Compute sin/cos/more with only shifts, adds and a small table - rotate a vector by shrinking angles. I-13 HAS multiply (*) but NOT shifts, so it cannot do the shift-and-add form. The irony: it has the expensive op, not the cheap one. Recommends shifts.

spheres.title: THE COLLATZ CONJECTURE
spheres.kicker: dart 010 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Lothar Collatz, 1937 (also Ulam / Kakutani / Syracuse / Thwaites)
spheres.i13_recommend: keep the panel's new % — parity is otherwise inexpressible
spheres.source: Lothar Collatz, 1937 (also Ulam / Kakutani / Syracuse / Thwaites)
spheres.blurb: The 3n+1 hailstone sequence (unproven since 1937, checked past 2^71). Even/odd is n % 2 - which I-13 could not do until the panel added %. Written in real I-13 with %, it RUNS (steps(27)=111). A dart where the wall came down: the technique named the gap, the panel filled it for one BinOp discriminant, the program runs.

spheres.title: THE FENWICK TREE
spheres.kicker: dart 011 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Boris Ryabko (1989) - before, and commonly mis-credited to, Peter Fenwick (1994)
spheres.i13_recommend: add bitwise ops now; treat an indexable array as a deliberate scope call
spheres.source: Boris Ryabko (1989) - before, and commonly mis-credited to, Peter Fenwick (1994)
spheres.blurb: The Binary Indexed Tree: O(log n) prefix sums via the low-bit trick i & (-i). It stacks TWO of I-13's walls - bitwise ops AND an array. Both proven absent on the live compiler (a & b -> E0001; a[0] -> E0001). Honest credit restores Ryabko before Fenwick.

spheres.title: SIMULATED ANNEALING
spheres.kicker: dart 012 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Kirkpatrick, Gelatt & Vecchi (1983); accept rule from Metropolis et al. (1953); Cerny (1985)
spheres.i13_recommend: keep random() rejected; ship a seeded LCG + exp as library defs
spheres.source: Kirkpatrick, Gelatt & Vecchi (1983); accept rule from Metropolis et al. (1953); Cerny (1985)
spheres.blurb: Probabilistic optimization that escapes local minima by accepting worse moves with probability e^(-dE/T) as temperature cools. Needs randomness + exp - I-13 has neither ambient. But a seeded LCG + Taylor exp written in pure I-13 CHECKS VALID and RUNS deterministically (byte-identical), vindicating 'seeded, not ambient'. (The mod it needs is the panel's new %.)

spheres.title: THE MONTY HALL PROBLEM
spheres.kicker: dart 013 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Steve Selvin (1975, coined the name); popularized by Marilyn vos Savant (1990)
spheres.i13_recommend: a seeded PRNG - the % it needs has now landed in the reference VM
spheres.source: Steve Selvin (1975, coined the name); popularized by Marilyn vos Savant (1990)
spheres.blurb: Three doors: switching wins 2/3, not 1/2. A 100k-game Monte-Carlo converges to 66.9% / 33.1% live. Needs a random source (I-13 refuses ambient random - E0202), but the seeded LCG that buys Monte-Carlo back deterministically now works, because DART 005's proposed % has since landed in the compiler. Proof that a dart's recommendation was implemented.

spheres.title: THE GAMBLER'S FALLACY
spheres.kicker: dart 014 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: the Monte Carlo fallacy - named for a 1913 roulette wheel that hit black 26 times
spheres.i13_recommend: a seeded PRNG; ties I-13's receipt discipline (no hidden state to carry a debt)
spheres.source: the Monte Carlo fallacy - named for a 1913 roulette wheel that hit black 26 times
spheres.blurb: The false belief that independent events 'balance out' - that black is 'due' after a run of red. A live fair-coin demo shows streaks are normal and the next flip stays 50/50. Needs a random source (seeded, per I-13's determinism). The deeper tie: I-13 has NO hidden state to carry a fallacious debt forward - exactly right.

spheres.title: DIJKSTRA'S SHUNTING-YARD
spheres.kicker: dart 015 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Edsger W. Dijkstra, 1961
spheres.i13_recommend: no change needed - this IS I-13's own precedence parser (a credit, not a gap)
spheres.blurb: Convert infix (3 + 4 * 2) to postfix via an operator stack + precedence - the classic precedence-parsing algorithm. Self-referential: I-13's OWN parser is a precedence parser (its infix table gives + - precedence 2, * / % precedence 3). So this is not a wall - it is how I-13 already parses. A dart that credits a strength; the new % slotted straight into that same table.

spheres.title: THE BOYER-MOORE MAJORITY VOTE
spheres.kicker: dart 016 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Robert S. Boyer & J Strother Moore, 1981
spheres.i13_recommend: an input/sequence story - the compute needs nothing new
spheres.source: Robert S. Boyer & J Strother Moore, 1981
spheres.blurb: Find a majority element in O(1) memory: a candidate + a counter, decrement on mismatch, swap when zero. The subtle finding: the ALGORITHM's state is two scalars, which I-13 handles fine - the wall is not the vote but the INPUT (I-13 has no arrays or I/O to feed it a stream). Distinguishes what I-13 can compute from what it can't yet express.

spheres.title: THE SIEVE OF ERATOSTHENES
spheres.kicker: dart 017 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Eratosthenes of Cyrene, c. 240 BC
spheres.i13_recommend: arrays for the sieve proper; % already enables trial-division primality
spheres.blurb: Mark the multiples of each prime; what stays unmarked is prime. Two angles: the classic sieve needs an ARRAY to mark composites (a wall - I-13 has no arrays), but trial-division primality (p % d == 0) needs only %, which the panel just added - so a prime test written in real I-13 with % RUNS. The sieve wants arrays; primality now runs.

spheres.title: BRAINFUCK
spheres.kicker: dart 018 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Urban Muller, 1993
spheres.i13_recommend: an indexed/tape aggregate (a deliberate scope call)
spheres.blurb: An esolang with 8 instructions on a tape of cells - Turing-complete. A mirror of I-13: 8 DESIGNED instructions vs I-13's 13 COUNTED symbols. BF's whole model is a tape (array) with a moving pointer, which I-13 cannot express (no arrays). Ties the repo's p-prime-prime -> BF esolang capstone.

spheres.title: THE MANDELBROT SET
spheres.kicker: dart 019 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Robert Brooks & Peter Matelski (1978); popularized by Benoit Mandelbrot (1980)
spheres.i13_recommend: no new feature for one point - only rendering a grid needs an array I-13 lacks
spheres.source: Robert Brooks & Peter Matelski (1978); popularized by Benoit Mandelbrot (1980)
spheres.blurb: The famous fractal: iterate z -> z^2 + c, escape or not. A rare NO-WALL dart - a complex number is just two f64 reals, and z^2+c uses only + - *, which I-13 HAS, so it can compute a point's escape count with two scalars and recursion. The only wall is OUTPUT (a grid render). Credits a strength.

spheres.title: CONWAY'S GAME OF LIFE
spheres.kicker: dart 020 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: John Conway, 1970 (published by Martin Gardner)
spheres.i13_recommend: a grid/array aggregate - a genuinely new kind of value
spheres.blurb: A cellular automaton: born on 3, survives on 2-3; from two rules emerge gliders and a universal Turing machine. Its state is a 2-D grid (an array) I-13 cannot hold. The deeper point: Life is Turing-complete by emergence, while I-13 is DELIBERATELY BOUNDED (the 4096-frame / 8M-step ceilings) - the opposite design stance.

spheres.title: THE LEVENSHTEIN DISTANCE
spheres.kicker: dart 021 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Vladimir Levenshtein, 1965
spheres.i13_recommend: a string/char type AND an array - expensive, likely a scope boundary
spheres.blurb: The minimum edits (insert/delete/substitute) between two strings, via a DP matrix. Stacks two I-13 walls at once: STRINGS (Constant is f64 only) and a 2-D DP ARRAY. Both proven absent on the live compiler. A recurring signal: I-13 keeps needing aggregates it has by design chosen not to have.

spheres.title: SOUNDEX
spheres.kicker: dart 022 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Robert C. Russell & Margaret King Odell (patented 1918)
spheres.i13_recommend: a string/char type - a scope question, not a bug
spheres.source: Robert C. Russell & Margaret King Odell (patented 1918)
spheres.blurb: A phonetic code: keep the first letter, map consonants to digits, drop vowels - so Robert and Rupert both become R163. Pure STRING work, per-character classification, which I-13 cannot express at all (no strings, no chars). I-13's numeric-scalar identity is exactly why text is out of reach.

spheres.title: DANCING LINKS
spheres.kicker: dart 023 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Donald Knuth, 2000 (Algorithm X / DLX)
spheres.i13_recommend: a reference/linked aggregate - a genuinely new kind of value
spheres.blurb: Knuth's technique for exact-cover (Sudoku, N-queens): circular doubly-linked lists let a column and its rows unlink and relink in O(1) - the links 'dance'. Pure POINTERS: I-13 has no references, no linked structures, only f64 scalars and functions. Knuth's elegance credited honestly.

spheres.title: GODEL NUMBERING
spheres.kicker: dart 024 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Kurt Godel, 1931
spheres.i13_recommend: the integer-exactness diagnostic (big Godel numbers blow past 2^53)
spheres.blurb: Godel's trick: encode a sequence of symbols as ONE integer via prime powers (2^a . 3^b ...); unique factorization decodes it back. Deeply self-referential for a COUNTED language - I-13's own 13 symbols could be Godel-numbered. Encoding needs only *; decoding needs the panel's new % to factor - but big numbers blow past f64's 2^53, tying I-13's counted identity, its %, and its f64 limit.

spheres.title: THE LINDENMAYER SYSTEM
spheres.kicker: dart 025 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Aristid Lindenmayer, 1968
spheres.i13_recommend: a string/sequence type - though the rewriting idea is already in I-13's pipeline
spheres.blurb: L-systems: parallel string rewriting (F -> F+F-F-F+F) grown from an axiom, drawn as turtle graphics - fractal plants and curves. String rewriting is the heart, which I-13 cannot hold (no strings). But the honest parallel: I-13 IS a symbol system with rewrite-like lowering (source -> AST -> IVM), so the concept is native; only the runtime string value is the wall.

spheres.title: NEWTON-RAPHSON METHOD
spheres.credit: Isaac Newton (1669) / Joseph Raphson (1690) / Thomas Simpson (1740)
spheres.i13_recommend: a statically-bounded loop (times N) so numeric iteration does not consume the 4096-frame recursion budget - a convenience, since everything here already runs on real I-13
spheres.blurb: Root-finding by tangent lines: stand on the curve, slide down the tangent to where it crosses zero, repeat - the correct digits double each step. A rare NO-WALL dart: real I-13 computes sqrt(2) to full f64 precision (root2 = 1.414213562373095), verified on the canonical H1.1 compiler via bounded recursion at call depth 21. The honest recommend is a statically-bounded loop so iteration stops eating the frame budget - a convenience, not new power; do not invent a wall that is not there. Credit is a three-way tangle: Newton (1669, unpublished till 1711), Raphson (1690, cleaner recursive form, ahead of Newton's OWN works; Wallis put the method into print first, 1685), Simpson (1740, the derivative form everyone actually uses).
spheres.kicker: dart 026 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: THE EUCLIDEAN ALGORITHM
spheres.credit: Euclid, Elements VII, c. 300 BC (older: Pythagorean anthyphairesis)
spheres.i13_recommend: % (modulo) - already built and tested on branch panel-recommends as bin::MOD, zero new alphabet symbols; turns Euclid's O(a+b) subtraction descent into O(log)
spheres.blurb: The greatest common divisor by repeated reduction - often called the oldest algorithm still in daily use. Euclid's ORIGINAL subtraction form runs unchanged in real I-13 (gcd(1071,462)=21, 252 steps, verified on the canonical compiler); the modern remainder form needs one operator, a mod b, which on main is an unexpected character but which the I-13 language panel already added as bin::MOD on branch panel-recommends (the full test suite passes). Recorded by Euclid in Elements VII (c.300 BC) but older still - Pythagorean anthyphairesis, reciprocal subtraction on lengths, alluded to by Aristotle before him.
spheres.kicker: dart 027 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: PERLIN NOISE
spheres.credit: Ken Perlin, 1983 (developed on Disney's TRON; Academy Award 1997)
spheres.i13_recommend: a bounded aggregate (fixed-size array, compile-time length, checked indexing) - or an on-record decision to declare aggregates permanently NOT COVERED; the most-requested feature across the whole dart campaign
spheres.blurb: The gradient noise that gave computer graphics its first believable clouds, marble, and terrain - invented by Ken Perlin WHILE working on Disney's TRON (1982), published at SIGGRAPH 1985, and given an Academy Award for Technical Achievement in 1997. World V is a TRON world, and this is where its look was born. A live animating field in TRON cyan and gold. It stands on a 256-entry permutation table, duplicated to 512 and indexed by hashed coordinates to pick each grid point's gradient - an array, the aggregate wall, which I-13 cannot express (check reports the unexpected character '['). The recommend is not 'add arrays' but 'decide, on the record, whether bounded aggregates are in scope, or declare them permanently NOT COVERED'.
spheres.kicker: dart 028 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: THE GAME OF NIM
spheres.credit: Charles L. Bouton, 1901 (generalized by Sprague 1935 & Grundy 1939)
spheres.i13_recommend: bitwise operators (^ & | >>) as new BinOp discriminants, zero new alphabet symbols - the SECOND dart to ask for bitwise (dart 001, fast inverse square root, was first); convergence is a signal
spheres.blurb: The founding game of combinatorial game theory - the first ever given a complete mathematical theory: take any number of tokens from one row, last to take wins. Charles Bouton (Harvard, 1901) named the game and proved the winning rule - the nim-sum, the bitwise XOR of the heap sizes, where zero means the player to move loses under perfect play. Playable live against a perfect machine. The entire theory is one XOR, which I-13 lacks (check reports the unexpected character '^') - the same bitwise wall that dart 001, the fast inverse square root, hit independently. Two darts converging on bitwise is a signal, not a coincidence. Sprague (1935) and Grundy (1939) later showed every impartial game reduces to a single Nim heap.
spheres.kicker: dart 029 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: BUFFON'S NEEDLE
spheres.credit: Comte de Buffon (posed 1733, solved 1777); Monte Carlo named by Ulam & Metropolis, 1940s
spheres.i13_recommend: a seeded PRNG as an ordinary I-13 function (dart 004 asked too - 2 darts converge); keeps determinism while unlocking the whole Monte Carlo family
spheres.blurb: The dart campaign's own metaphor, from 1777: drop needles on a lined floor, count how many cross a line, and pi falls out of pure chance - the FIRST Monte Carlo method, ~170 years before Metropolis named it (for the casino where Ulam's uncle gambled; von Neumann designed the first ENIAC run, coded by Metropolis and Klara von Neumann). Given the crossing count, pi is one division and I-13 computes it on main (pi = 3.1416902..., verified); but the random throw itself is the wall - I-13 has no randomness at all, by design. Recommend a seeded PRNG (dart 004 asked too), keeping determinism while unlocking Monte Carlo. Credit: Buffon posed 1733, solved 1777 in Essai d'arithmetique morale; Laplace 1812 noted it estimates pi.
spheres.kicker: dart 030 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: THE METROPOLIS-HASTINGS ALGORITHM
spheres.credit: Metropolis, A. Rosenbluth, M. Rosenbluth, A. Teller, E. Teller (1953); Hastings (1970) - code by Arianna Rosenbluth
spheres.i13_recommend: a transcendental library WRITTEN IN I-13 (exp/ln/sin/cos as bounded Taylor sums of + - * /, zero new opcodes) plus the seeded PRNG
spheres.blurb: How to sample a distribution you can only score, never invert: take a random walk that accepts good steps always and bad steps sometimes, and the walk's footprints reproduce the distribution - the engine of modern Bayesian statistics. The honest-credit story: the 1953 paper's real coder was Arianna W. Rosenbluth, who wrote the actual MANIAC code and ran the computations; Marshall Rosenbluth (physics; a key weighting insight came from Edward Teller) recalled 'we never had a single scientific discussion with him' about Metropolis, who ran the computer lab. Her authorship was under-credited for half a century before being restored. W. K. Hastings generalized it in 1970. I-13 walls: exp (E0202 unknown function) and randomness - recommend a transcendental library written IN I-13 (exp/ln/sin/cos are bounded Taylor sums of the four arithmetic ops, zero new opcodes) plus the seeded PRNG.
spheres.kicker: dart 031 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: THE RABIN-MILLER PRIMALITY TEST
spheres.credit: Gary Miller (1976, deterministic under ERH) & Michael Rabin (1980, randomized)
spheres.i13_recommend: arbitrary-precision integers (f64 overflows past 2^53) + a seeded PRNG for witnesses; modexp itself now RUNS thanks to the merged %
spheres.blurb: Tell if a huge number is prime without factoring it: interrogate it with random witnesses; each honest witness that fails to expose it halves your doubt (false-prime chance below 4^-k). It never proves primality, only makes composite-ness astronomically unlikely - and it correctly catches Carmichael numbers like 561 that fool the Fermat test (verified in the live demo, witness a=337). spheres.title: THE HAMMING (7,4) CODE

spheres.title: THE REFLECTED BINARY (GRAY) CODE

The Gray (reflected binary) code reorders the counts so exactly ONE bit changes between neighbours - and the whole thing is one line, gray(n) = n ^ (n>>1), which I-13 now computes (gray of 4,5,6,7 = 6,7,5,4, verified). Credit is a naming accident: named for Frank Gray (Bell Labs, patent 1953) but Emile Baudot used a reflected binary code in his 1878 telegraph, and the single-change ordering is in the centuries-old Baguenaudier (Chinese rings) puzzle. spheres.title: FLOYD'S CYCLE DETECTION
spheres.credit: attributed to Robert W. Floyd (unsourced); Brent's variant 1980

It runs in I-13 as plain recursion carrying the two positions (meet=2, verified). The credit is a mystery, the inverse of this campaign's usual bug: called 'Floyd's cycle detection', but Robert Floyd apparently never published it - the attribution traces to Knuth (TAOCP) with no citation, and no Floyd paper has been found; it seems to be folklore pinned to a famous name. Richard Brent published a genuinely faster, properly-cited variant in 1980. The honest label is 'the tortoise and the hare', after Aesop. spheres.title: THE KARATSUBA ALGORITHM

The recursion runs in real I-13 (Karatsuba split of 1234*5678 = 7006652 = direct, verified) via %, /, and recursion. Credit given generously: Andrey Kolmogorov conjectured multiplication requires Omega(n^2) at a Moscow seminar; Anatoly Karatsuba, 23, found the three-multiply split within a week, disproving it; Kolmogorov wrote it up himself in 1962 UNDER KARATSUBA'S NAME, and Karatsuba only learned it was published from the reprints mailed to him. It opened fast algorithms (Toom-Cook, Schonhage-Strassen, Harvey-van der Hoeven 2019). The recommend is the WITHHELD arbitrary-precision integers - and Karatsuba is the sharpest case yet: it exists FOR thousand-digit numbers where it beats schoolbook, but on f64's ~15 exact digits there is nothing big enough to be worth it. It RUNS in real I-13 now on the new bounded array (found 23 at index 5, verified), where every index is BOUNDS-CHECKED (out-of-range -> clean E0501) - exactly the discipline the famous overflow bug lacked, and impossible to reproduce here. spheres.title: THE FISHER-YATES SHUFFLE

The obvious way - swap each card with a random one from the whole deck - is subtly BIASED (n^n equally-likely runs cannot divide evenly into n! orderings, so some permutations are over-represented). Fisher-Yates picks the swap partner from 0..i only, giving exactly n! equal outcomes. It is the dart where TWO campaign additions to I-13 meet: the ARRAY (to swap in place) and the seeded PRNG (std/rng_lcg). It runs - a valid permutation of 0..7, sum stays 28, verified. The campaign's cleanest convergence: random (darts 004/030) and aggregates (017/028) both landed, and Fisher-Yates is where they shake hands.

It RUNS in real I-13 over the new array (best=6 for [-2,1,-3,4,-1,2,1,-5,4], the run [4,-1,2,1], verified) - an algorithm that was pure 'aggregate wall' a day ago now runs unchanged from its textbook form. spheres.title: THE QUICKSORT
spheres.credit: Tony Hoare, 1959-61 (Moscow, machine translation)

Tony Hoare (1959), an exchange student in Kolmogorov's milieu (the same seminar culture that produced Karatsuba, dart 041), needed to sort words to look them up in a Russian-English dictionary for machine translation; he had the idea but could not write it down until he learned ALGOL 60's recursion, and published it as Algorithm 64 in 1961. Its LOMUTO PARTITION runs in real I-13 on the new array (pivot=5, smaller elements moved to the front, verified). But full quicksort's recursion needs the partition to return TWO things at once - the rearranged array AND the pivot's final index - and an I-13 function returns exactly one value. That is the NEWEST wall in the whole campaign, and it is telling: the array the author just added cleared the aggregate wall, and the very next classic algorithm reveals the edge behind it. Recommend: a way to return multiple values (a small tuple/pair). A sort DOES run today (bubble and insertion thread a single array cleanly, verified); quicksort specifically wants the dual return. Two open recommends now stand: multiple return (this dart) and bignum (darts 032/035/036/041).

It RUNS in real I-13 over the new array (distB=2 via 0->2->1, verified). Credit is shared four ways: Alfonso Shimbel 1955 (earliest), Lester Ford Jr. 1956, Edward F. Moore 1957 (the BFS variant), Richard Bellman 1958 (who coined 'dynamic programming'); the name honors only two. It is dynamic programming over a table, and the bounded array is exactly that table.

CE) posed and answered it; Aryabhata used a related method (kuttaka) in 6th-c. India; Qin Jiushao gave the general 'Da Yan' algorithm in 1247; Gauss formalized it in Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801), 1,500 years after Sunzi. spheres.title: UNION-FIND (THE DISJOINT SET)
spheres.credit: Galler & Fischer 1964; Tarjan's inverse-Ackermann analysis 1975

spheres.blurb: Track who belongs to which group as groups keep merging - connected components, Kruskal's spanning trees - answering 'same group?' in almost constant time, from ONE array of parent pointers. Basic union-find RUNS in real I-13 on the new array (union 0-1, 2-3, 1-3; then 0 and 2 share a set, 0 and 5 don't, verified). Credit: Bernard Galler & Michael Fischer described it 1964 (for a FORTRAN equivalence problem); Robert Tarjan proved in 1975 that m operations cost O(m*alpha(n)) with union-by-rank + path compression, alpha the inverse Ackermann function (effectively <= 4 for any n in the universe) - a famously tight, hard-won bound. But path compression wants find() to return BOTH the root AND the rewired array - two values - the exact MULTIPLE-RETURN wall quicksort (dart 045) hit. spheres.title: THE COUNTING SORT
spheres.credit: Harold H. Seward, 1954
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - the MOST NATURAL fit for a bounded array: counting sort needs an array sized to a known bound (the value range), which is exactly what I-13's array is; no comparisons, just indexed writes into a bounded table
spheres.blurb: Every sort you've seen compares pairs of elements, and no comparison sort can beat n log n. Counting sort never compares anything: it tallies how many of each value there are, then reads them out in order - linear time when the values live in a known range, and the PERFECT fit for I-13's bounded array, whose length is fixed and known. It RUNS in real I-13 (sort [4,2,7,2,0,5,2,9] -> 0,2,2,2,4,5,7,9, verified) via a tally array (one bucket per value) and an output array, both bounded. Credit: Harold H. Seward, 1954 MIT master's thesis (which also introduced radix sort) - sorting by distribution, not comparison, stepping outside the decision-tree model that forces Omega(n log n) on comparison sorts. Of all the array darts, this is the most natural fit: where quicksort strained against the language, counting sort fits it like a glove - no comparisons, just indexed writes into a bounded table.
